concept.name: Core-satellite approach
concept.definition: A portfolio-construction framework that places the majority of assets in a low-cost, passively managed core tracking broad market indexes, surrounded by smaller actively managed satellite positions intended to add alpha or diversification. It blends passive efficiency with bounded active risk.
concept.intuition: Lock in the market return on most of the money and confine your bets to a satellite sleeve, where manager skill or concentrated themes can only help or hurt at the margin.
concept.mechanics: Allocate the core to index funds or ETFs (e.g., an S&P 500 tracker) and the satellites to active funds, sectors, or strategies (high-yield bonds, biotech, commodities), then rebalance to hold the split. The core minimizes costs and portfolio beta while satellites carry the tracking error.
concept.failure_modes: Poor satellite selection or an excessive satellite weight erodes the cost and risk benefits, effectively recreating an expensive active portfolio; persistent active underperformance drags total return below the cheap index the core was meant to secure.
concept.misconceptions: That the framework itself generates outperformance; it is an organizational discipline - the satellites still must earn their fees, and most active managers do not beat their benchmarks net of costs.
concept.example: 50% in an S&P 500 index fund as the core, with 10% in an actively managed high-yield bond fund, 20% in a biotechnology fund, and 20% in a commodities fund as satellites (Investopedia illustration).
